1:
What the opening noun means governs how the whole chapter reads. Keil and Delitzsch insist it denotes not a station but the striking of a camp, and so a train or march; the itinerary consequently describes Israel's progress by the spots they left rather than the spots they occupied, which is why the refrain throughout is that they broke up. Ellicott takes the word the same way, adding that these encampments lasted very unequal periods and, through the long wandering, may have averaged a twelvemonth apiece. Calvin makes the same distinction his key: marches are set against stations, and Israel struck camp only when the cloud lifted from the sanctuary and moved elsewhere, as though God stretched a hand out of heaven to point their road.

Why so full a list appears now, when earlier narrative gave only the memorable halts, is Calvin's question. Previously Moses had recorded scarcely more than the places where something notable happened; here he names every stopping-place, painting the forty years as a picture. Three purposes govern that, on Calvin's reading. Local description lends certainty to history, so the memory of the rescue would be pressed deeper. The names themselves recall how often and how variously the nation had provoked God. Above all, standing at the very threshold of Canaan, they were meant to recognise that their own depravity and stubbornness had held them back and sent them wandering by tortuous routes — while recognising too that God so tempered the punishment as to preserve the despisers of his grace, and carried forward to their children the covenant made with Abraham.

Ellicott balances the same two faces of the record: it stands as a permanent memorial of the nation's sin and rebellion on one side, and of God's faithfulness and long-suffering in leading and sustaining them on the other.

How the register came to be written interests Henry more than what it contains. God ordered Moses at the outset to keep a journal, entering the remarkable occurrences of the way, so that reviewing it might satisfy him and publishing it might instruct others. Henry turns that into advice: private Christians, and men in public station especially, do well to preserve some written account of God's providences toward them, the steady run of mercies received and the turns that made certain days memorable — for our memories are treacherous and want the help. Wesley repeats the counsel almost word for word.

One clause carries an ambiguity nobody resolves. Gill offers both constructions: either the journeys themselves were made at God's commandment, which is how Aben Ezra joins the words and which the narrative elsewhere states plainly, since they halted while the cloud rested and moved when it rose; or else Moses wrote the account at God's commandment, so that it might stand on record for later ages and prove that Israel really had been led about a wilderness whose places bore no names but the ones they gave them. Ellicott states the alternative and declines to choose between them.

Clarke, characteristically, thinks about the document as a document. The book may fairly be considered a diary, and indeed the first book of travels ever published; Shaw, Pococke and others have tried to plot the route, and enough evidence survives that many stages can be identified from descriptions particular enough to fix them, though by no means all. He allows a broad typology — Israel was the church of God in the wilderness, and its unsettled wandering answers to the unsettled state of religion under the law, as the entry into rest under Joshua answers to the fixed salvation provided by Christ, of whom Joshua was in name and conduct a type. But he refuses to follow that further, and says so bluntly of those who do.
3:
Where the nation actually assembled draws a small argument. Gill takes Rameses for the Egyptian city in which Israel seems to have been gathered into one body shortly before departure so as to march out together, and reports two identifications — the Targum of Jonathan's Pelusium, and Dr Shaw's guess at Cairo. Clarke calls it the metropolis of Goshen and the rendezvous of the whole nation, and likewise supposes it Cairo. Calvin objects to a third view, that the name stands for the entire land of Goshen: it is unreasonable to imagine them setting out simultaneously from scattered and distant places, and less reasonable still given that they went forth in orderly array. He does not require the whole multitude inside the walls, which could hardly have held them, but supposes Moses and Aaron mustered them in the neighbourhood so that the column might be organised, lest a hurried march become a confusion in which each hindered the rest.

That the departure happened in full view of Egypt is pressed for what it proves. Calvin reads the witnesses as evidence of surrender: the Egyptians had by then abandoned the contest, so thoroughly subdued that they dared not raise a finger. He is careful about the reason, though. Moses does not say they refrained from obstruction because burying their dead left them no leisure; the point is rather that grief exasperated them and yet they lay stupefied, God's power having drained away their capacity to resist. Gill puts the practical side plainly — hearts heavy, hands full, other work in front of them — and adds that the Egyptians knew perfectly well why the blow had fallen, since it was for detaining Israel.

Judgment on the gods of Egypt is the clause that divides them. Wesley takes it concretely and doubly: the false gods were the beasts those brutish worshippers adored, and these died with the rest when the firstborn of man and beast were struck; their images too, he thinks, were probably thrown down, as Dagon afterwards fell before the ark. Calvin will have none of it. To imagine that every idol in Egypt toppled of its own accord he calls a silly notion; what the phrase means is that God triumphed over them by demonstrating effectively that they could not help their worshippers, and by exposing the magicians' trickery at the same time.

Calvin then explains why the point was worth making at all. The clause is there to commend the true faith and to fence Israel against ever drifting into Gentile superstition, since at the moment of their rescue they had seen those superstitions proved empty. Pharaoh and his forces were not the only casualties: the gods who claimed to guard that land were shamed with them, and every superstition attached to them stood convicted of folly. To this, Calvin thinks, Isaiah alludes when he foretells that the Lord shall come into Egypt and the idols of Egypt be moved at his presence — meaning that God would give such proofs of power there as would demonstrate the emptiness of all those errors and overturn the fictions by which Israel themselves had been deceived.
5:
Gill measures the itinerary in miles where Clarke identifies its sites, and they rarely overlap. Eight miles carried Israel from Succoth to Etham, sixteen more to Pihahiroth, eight from Marah to Elim, six from Elim to the sea, sixteen thence to the wilderness of Sin, twelve from Dophkah to Alush, and eight apiece for the last two stages to Rephidim and Sinai. Clarke numbers the stations and asks what each name attaches to. Succoth means booths, and probably denotes no settlement but simply where tents first went up after Rameses. Etham he cannot place: Shaw put it a mile from Cairo, Calmet identified it with the Buthum of Herodotus on Arabia's Egyptian frontier, and made Baal-zephon the Clysma of the Greeks and Kolzum of the Arabs. Dophkah and Alush, absent from Exodus, he gives up as unknown.

A turn in the route needs explaining, and Gill explains it away. Aben Ezra referred it either to the cloud or to Israel; Gill thinks it covers both, since Israel turned as the cloud turned and was directed by it. What it does not mean is that they had reached Pihahiroth already and doubled back — they simply swung out of the direct road toward it, and the word rendered again would be better dropped. Why they left Gill states baldly: Pharaoh's army was pressing on them.

Some stations bring their own histories. Gill notes that the halt by the sea goes unmentioned in Exodus, that the departure from the wilderness of Sin followed the manna, and that the Targum of Jonathan renders Alush the strong fort — where, on the Jewish chronology he reports, Israel first kept a sabbath. Of Sinai he says only what happened there: from that mountain came the decalogue with every statute judicial and ceremonial, and the directions for the tabernacle and its vessels, all made during the stay.

Clarke's traveller's notes are more exact and less reverent. Marah he places at Sedur on Shaw's authority, opposite the valley of Baideah, and observes that the wilderness of Etham is called the wilderness of Shur in Exodus. At Elim, two leagues from Tor and nearly thirty from Corondel, Shaw counted only nine of the twelve wells the text names but upwards of two thousand palms in place of seventy. The wilderness of Sin lies between Elim and the mountain, and Shaw's party crossed it in nine hours. The encampment by the sea Clarke finds hardest, since Israel was by then bearing east toward Sinai and moving further from the water; he supposes it took the name from having the sea still in view, and notes that it appears nowhere else. He also protests the name. Nothing about that water or its sand is red; the Hebrew means the weedy sea, and the Greek version turned it red, the Latin followed, and the European translations followed the Latin — in opposition, he says, to etymology and reason alike.

Calvin reads the same stages for what they cost and proved. The three days' march celebrates God's power rather than the people's endurance, for between the sea and Marah no water was found at all, which makes their impiety the more detestable when they rebelled over a bitter taste; and God's mercy shone the brighter in refreshing such churlish and provoking men at a station of twelve springs and seventy palms. He notices what Moses passes over — the wilderness of Sin gets a bare line, though the people's impiety betrayed itself there and the place was ennobled by manna, so that mortal men ate angels' food; Rephidim's want of water is barely adverted to; only at the Graves of Concupiscence is a memorial of punishment inscribed in the name itself. From that reticence Calvin draws his conclusion: since the other places are listed without their events, Moses meant nothing more than to set the forty years' wandering before the nation's eyes.
16:
The first name in this stretch carries its own story. Gill explains that here the people lusted after flesh and murmured, and though the flesh came a pestilence came with it and destroyed many, who were buried on the spot — whence a name meaning the graves of lust, that is, of those who lusted. Clarke insists it was no city or village but bare desert, taking its name from the plague that answered their murmuring and inordinate craving.

Taberah's absence from the list troubles both, and they account for it differently. Gill offers two explanations: either Taberah was the same place as Kibroth-hattaavah or lay close beside it, or, as Aben Ezra says, Israel camped there a single day and so it does not rank among the journeys, though it was one of the three stages between Sinai and the graves. Clarke reasons from the distance instead. Israel had covered three days' march to reach this point, from which he infers that other stations must have stood between and gone unrecorded here, probably because they were nowhere remarkable.

Hazeroth passes quickly. Gill puts it eight miles on and remembers it as the place where Miriam was struck with leprosy; Clarke reports Shaw's computation of some thirty miles from Sinai.

Rithmah gets the fullest treatment, partly because its name is transparent. Both take the root for juniper, Clarke supposing the site named from the abundance of those trees somewhere in the wilderness of Paran, Gill quoting the Targum of Jonathan's gloss that juniper grew there. Gill then cites travellers who found the valley still called Ritma, named in their account from a yellow flower that carpets it, and who came upon two cisterns of excellent water on the left hand — which may be exactly why Israel pitched there. He also reports a bolder identification: some learned men make Rithmah the same as Kadesh-barnea, from which the spies were sent, since that was the next remove from Hazeroth as this is, and Jarchi finds the name apt for the very reason, the evil tongue of the spies answering to the psalm's sharp arrows of the mighty with coals of juniper. Josephus, Gill adds, may be naming the same place Dathema.

After that the list runs dry, and Gill and Clarke fail it in opposite directions. Gill keeps counting: six miles apiece from Rithmah to Rimmon-parez, thence to Libnah, Rissah, Kehelathah and Shapher, then four to Haradah, four and a half to Makheloth, four each to Tahath, Tarah and Mithcah, and eight to Hashmonah. Clarke can only record ignorance, and does so without embroidery. Libnah is uncertain, though Joshua names a town of that name between Kadesh-barnea and Gaza. Rissah occurs nowhere else in Scripture and its site is utterly uncertain. Kehelathah is utterly unknown, and the conjecture that it might be Keilah he thinks unlikely. Where mount Shapher lay cannot be determined. Haradah is unknown, though Calmet suggested the Bered of Genesis, near Kadesh. Makheloth is found nowhere else at all.
28:
Clarke keeps guessing where guessing is possible. Mithcah he leaves to Calmet, who conjectured the Mocha of Arabia Petraea; Hashmonah some have taken for the Azmon named in the next chapter; Hor-hagidgad means the pit or hole of Gidgad and was perhaps distinguished by some vast cavern, though where it stood nobody knows. Jotbathah is likewise unplaced, but Deuteronomy calls it a land of rivers of waters. Ebronah occurs nowhere else. Bene-jaakan, the sons of Jaakan, is unknown.

Two stations he can fix, and both matter. Ezion-gaber Shaw put on the western shore of the Elantic gulf, some sixty miles from Sinai, and the Arabs call it still the golden port, since Solomon's ships sailed from there for the gold of Ophir. Zin, which the text identifies with Kadesh, Clarke remembers for Miriam's death and the water struck from the rock; and because it lay on Edom's border, and passage through Edom was refused although that road ran straight for Canaan, Israel had to bear right toward Mount Hor, which the Arabs now call Accaba.

Where Aaron died raises a real difficulty, since Deuteronomy tells the sequence differently. Gill reports it plainly: that book names the place Mosera, and has Israel arriving there from Bene-jaakan, whereas this chapter has them leaving Hashmonah for Moseroth and reaching Bene-jaakan afterwards. His solution, which he takes from Jarchi, is that they doubled back — Hashmonah to Mosera, then Bene-jaakan, then Mosera again — the two places lying twenty-four miles apart. Clarke resolves it by geography instead. Since Deuteronomy places Aaron's death at Mosera and this chapter places it at Hor, either Mosera, Moseroth and Hor are three names for one site, or Moseroth was a town or village standing near the mountain.

Gill goes on counting where Clarke goes on identifying, and his figures grow longer as the wandering does: thirty-two miles from Hashmonah to Moseroth, twenty from Bene-jaakan to Hor-hagidgad — which the Targum of Jonathan calls Gudgod and Deuteronomy Gudgodah — then twenty-four to Jotbathah, twenty more to Ebronah, twenty-eight to Ezion-geber, forty-eight to the wilderness of Zin, and forty-eight again to Mount Hor. Keil and Delitzsch, for their part, decline to treat the remaining names here at all, referring each of them back to the narrative chapters where the events belonging to them were recorded.

Aaron's death gets the fullest notice in the stretch. Gill supplies the arithmetic of his hundred and twenty-three years — eighty-three when he stood before Pharaoh, and forty since spent with Israel — and observes that he was three years the elder of Moses. Calvin asks why the age is stated at all, and answers that it belongs to the argument. At a hundred Aaron had already outrun the ordinary span, yet by an extraordinary blessing he was kept alive until the nation stood on the very edge of its inheritance; and since God preserved the minister of his grace so long precisely for their advantage, their failure to acknowledge that fatherly care was the baser for it.

The chapter's last incident before the plains of Moab is a battle it does not describe. Calvin notes that Moses gives no account of the fighting and merely revives the recollection, the point being that at this stage of the march Israel at last encountered an enemy and began to engage one of the nations of Canaan. That, on his reading, is the whole significance of the notice: it marks the opening of their warfare, at the moment when the land promised them as an inheritance was about to be entered and taken.
41:
Clarke reads the first names of this last stretch etymologically. Zalmonah he places somewhere near Edom and derives from the word for an image, guessing that the brazen serpent Moses set up gave the site its name — from the same root, he adds, comes the term corrupted into talisman, meaning a consecrated image. Punon is a place in Idumea mentioned nowhere else; Oboth has appeared before. Ije-abarim, the heaps of Abarim, he cannot locate, but since the word means heaps or protuberances he supposes low mounds near a Jordan ford, and notes that the next verse shortens the name to Iim.

Two accounts of this leg do not match, and Ellicott's longest note in the chapter reconciles them. The earlier narrative lists seven stations between Ije-abarim and the plains of Moab; here only three appear, and not one of the three shares a name with the seven. On the count, he proposes that the earlier chapter records only stations of historical importance — those from which some military expedition set out — whereas this one records every place where an organised camp was pitched and the tent of meeting formally raised. On the names, he appeals to scale: six hundred thousand men with wives, children and cattle must have spread over a wide area, and in settled country could have occupied several towns at once — as this chapter shows, camping them from Beth-jesimoth all the way to Abel-shittim. Dibon of Gad may therefore answer to one or more of the sites north of the Arnon, and Almon-diblathaim, which seems to have lain north or north-west of Dibon, to Bamoth. About the last he has no doubt: the mountains of Abarim before Nebo are the valley in the field of Moab at the top of Pisgah, since Nebo was a peak of Pisgah, Pisgah one of the mountains of Abarim, and Moses' burial place is described as the valley in the land of Moab.

Gill reaches a similar result by a shorter road. From Almon-diblathaim, he observes, the earlier account has Israel going on to Beer — a place named from the well they found there — along with several other removes which this chapter omits, and he supposes those were short shifts of camp rather than stations properly so called. He also explains the compound name: the valley of Zared held Dibon-gad, which perhaps took its second element from Gad's rebuilding it later. Ellicott refers the name to the Gadites' fortifying of Dibon on the northern bank of the Arnon, one of the towns Reuben and Gad had asked for.

The last stages are given their histories rather than their coordinates. Clarke notes that Almon-diblathaim was Moabite territory in Jeremiah's day and its position now unknown; that the mountains of Abarim are where Moses died, reached after the overthrow of the Amorites; and that the plains of Moab were the scene of everything that passed between Balaam and Balak. Gill measures each of those removes at sixteen miles, derives Abarim from the nearby Jordan crossings, and fixes the final camp by Eusebius — ten miles from Jericho, on the far side of the river.

How wide that final camp stretched, and what its second name means, close the itinerary. Gill reports the common Jewish estimate that it reached twelve miles, the Jerusalem Targum putting the question and answering it in those terms. Abel-shittim, he explains, is sometimes simply Shittim, from the wood that grew there; the prefix means mourning, and commemorates the grief that followed the plague in which twenty-four thousand died. Wesley gives the same account of the name and attaches it to the sin in the matter of Peor. Clarke ends where the march does — Beth-jesimoth afterwards fell to the Reubenites, and Israel now stood at the edge of Jordan, opposite the Jericho they would later cross to.
50:
Keil and Delitzsch treat the closing verses as one command in two halves: exterminate the Canaanites, and divide their land among Israel's families. Crossing the Jordan, the nation was to destroy the inhabitants and every memorial of their idolatry, then take possession and settle, since Jehovah had given the country to them for a possession. They note that one Hebrew verb carries both movements — to take possession of, and so to drive others out of possession, to exterminate. Gill adds the setting and audience: the word came in the plains of Moab by Jordan near Jericho, and concerned the whole body of the people.

Calvin insists that the two halves belong together and refuses to let them be separated. He has explained elsewhere why God willed these nations expelled — lest they adulterate his pure worship by their admixtures, corrupt Israel by bad example, and stand as pollutions in a holy land. Here, though, Moses is making a different point. About to describe how the country would be divided, he begins by saying it must first be emptied, so that its free and full enjoyment might remain for the children of Israel. The clauses run on together — dispossess the inhabitants and dwell there, for I have given you the land to possess it — and Calvin thinks it would be absurd to detach the one from the other, since the gift is what makes the dispossession intelligible.

Henry reads the command against the forty years that preceded it, and finds a purpose in the wandering itself. While Israel was in the wilderness their total separation from every other people kept them clear of the temptation to idolatry; perhaps that was one thing intended by the long confinement, so that the idols of Egypt might be forgotten, the nation aired and purified of the infection, and the generation that entered Canaan be men who had never known those depths of Satan. Crossing Jordan meant walking back into that temptation, which is why the charge comes now.

What that charge required Henry states without softening. They were not merely to expel the inhabitants and occupy the country; they were to deface every idolatrous picture and image and pull down every high place, preserving nothing whatever. Not as monuments of antiquity, to gratify the curious. Not as ornaments for their houses. Not as toys for their children. Everything was to go — partly as declared abhorrence and detestation of idolatry, and partly to remove the temptation, whether to worship those images and the false gods they stood for, or to worship the God of Israel by such representations.

Obedience and disobedience are given their consequences in turn, and Henry states both as maxims. Keep clear of the idols of Canaan, and God will by degrees put you in full possession of Canaan's wealth: learn not their way, and then fear not their power. Spare either the idols or the idolaters, and you will be beaten with your own rod, your sin becoming your punishment. Israel would then be fostering snakes in their own bosoms, since any league with the remnant — even a bare cessation of arms — would leave them pricks in the eyes and thorns in the sides, insulting, robbing, making what mischief they could. We must expect trouble from whatever we sinfully indulge, Henry concludes; what we are willing should tempt us we shall find will vex us. And the righteous God would turn upon Israel the very wheel that was to have crushed the Canaanites, since if they fell in with those nations and learned their ways his displeasure would justly be greater against them than against the Canaanites themselves. Let us hear this and fear: if we do not drive sin out, sin will drive us out, and if we are not the death of our lusts, our lusts will be the death of our souls.
52:
What exactly was to be destroyed occupies four of them, differing in emphasis rather than substance. Clarke derives the word rendered pictures from a root meaning to resemble, and thinks it covers pictures, carved work or embroidery alike, so far as such things displayed the abominations of idolatry; the molten images he takes for metallic talismanic figures, cast under particular constellations and credited with extraordinary virtues. Ellicott renders the same word imagery or engraved figures, and observes that where Leviticus names the material it is stone, shaped into an idol. Keil and Delitzsch divide the terms by material: a stone idol, images cast from brass, and bamoth, the Canaanite altars raised on high ground. Ellicott takes the high places the same way, referring the phrase to the altars built on them.

How thoroughly the inhabitants were to be removed is put two ways. Gill reads the command as an aim rather than an event: not accomplished at once but gradually, Israel using their utmost endeavours toward complete extirpation. Wesley is blunter — driving out means not banishing but destroying — and defines the furniture as he goes: the pictures stones curiously engraven and set up for worship, the high places chapels, altars, groves or whatever else had been erected for worship there. Gill's note on the dispossession keeps the plain sense: turn them out of their cities, towns and houses, and live in them.

The division by lot repeats an earlier command verbatim, Keil and Delitzsch observe, and they give the idiom literally — whatever the lot coming out of the urn points to shall be that family's portion.

Calvin asks why a lottery, and answers first from human nature. No tribe would have submitted to being sent here or there at another man's option, and had the arrangement been left to the judges' votes they would have quarrelled rather than settled what was right. But something deeper lies underneath. By this method God proved that Israel held the land as inheritors and masters by his liberality and special blessing; for though men reckon nothing more fortuitous than a lot, the lot is governed by God, as Solomon says. He commanded the casting and reserved the outcome to himself. How else did Zebulun receive his portion on the sea-shore, except that Jacob had foretold it? Why did the best corn country fall to Asher, unless because the same lips had said his bread should be fat and he should yield royal dainties? By the same prophecy Judah drew an inheritance rich in vines and pasture.

From that Calvin draws two conclusions. The division proved that God had not promised the land to Abraham in vain, since what Jacob had proclaimed was confirmed in the event — and Jacob was a man famine had driven out, a sojourner in Egypt and twice an exile, who nonetheless allotted portions to his descendants as authoritatively as a father parcelling a few acres among heirs. What might then have looked ridiculous God sealed at last. Things we take, in the feebleness of our senses, to move at the blind impulse of chance are directed by his secret providence, his counsel running so regular a course that the end answers to the beginning. Calvin adds the rule of proportion — larger or smaller allotments according to numbers — and then refuses an allegory plausible only at first glance. Some read the lot as figuring how we obtain a heavenly inheritance by God's gratuitous good pleasure; Calvin answers that the facts will not carry it. Hebron belonged to the inheritance, yet Caleb received it without any lot, and Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh took all the territory won beyond Jordan by the consent of the rest rather than by lot at all. Let readers abstain from such conceits, he concludes, lest they be obliged to confess with shame that they have caught at an empty shadow.
55:
Gill defines the failure before the punishment. Not driving them out means being remiss and careless, indifferent to the business, declining the proper means of getting rid of them — or worse, striking covenants with them, intermarrying, growing friendly, and suffering them to remain.

Calvin weighs the guilt on both sides. That God's anger against these nations should have burned so hot is no mystery: gross indulgence of sin had begun to prevail among them as far back as Abraham's day, which is why God then said their iniquity was not yet full, and after four hundred years of abused forbearance nobody can deny that destruction was the just reward of so long an obstinacy. Even in cutting them off, though, God had his elect people in view, that Israel might be kept separate and never turn aside to foreign superstitions. Israel's own remissness therefore deserved the threatened punishment twice over. They failed in the duty of executing God's vengeance, and so far as lay with them detracted from his grace — no common honour having been conferred when he made them ministers of his judgments, base supineness was the worst possible response. They had been given the whole land, and by contenting themselves with part of it and neglecting the rest they betrayed a perverse ingratitude. And they wilfully entangled themselves by mixing with nations God had separated them from precisely so that their habits and their rites should not be imitated.

What the threatened nations became is a matter of record. Calvin points to Judges for the clearest and amplest testimony that the sentence took effect, and observes that the infliction on their eyes and sides was still running as late as David's reign — which proves how untamable their headstrongness was, since an admonition so solemn failed to move them forward either in victory or in the punishing of crimes over which they had been made judges.

Clarke works the metaphor itself. Nothing is more vexatious than a continual goading on both sides, so that the attempt to escape the one throws the body harder against the other; nothing more distressing than a perpetual pricking in the eye, which harasses the mind, torments the body and puts out the sight. He notes that pious men have long taken the surviving Canaanites for an emblem of indwelling sin, and thinks the comparison holds for anyone who will not have the blood of the covenant cleanse him. While conscience stays tender such a man feels straitened in all his goings and hindered in every religious service; then, fatally persuaded that sin must dwell in him as long as he lives, he adjusts his mind to the situation, his conscience loses its tenderness, and he settles for expecting redemption where and when it was never promised — beyond the grave.

Gill and Ellicott close the chapter on the same historical note. Gill spells out the mechanism: suffering the Canaanites to remain, mingling with them, learning their works and serving their gods, Israel would be delivered into enemy hands and carried captive into other lands. Ellicott would render the last verse as a comparison rather than a sequel — as I have determined to do unto them, so will I do unto you — and observes what the history bears out, that the idolaters of Canaan were never wholly exterminated, that their pernicious influence was felt through the whole of Israel's story, and that the threatened judgments were executed at last in the Assyrian and Babylonian captivities.
